Reinhold Messner: Italian mountaineer, adventurer and explorer (born 1944)

Born when Octavian rose to power and established the Augustan Principate in 27 BC, its western half fell in 476 AD while its eastern half lived on until Constantinople fell in 1453. What state is this?
Roman Empire: 27 BC–476/1453 AD state and civilization. The Roman Empire was a state that dominated the Mediterranean and much of Europe, Western Asia, and North Africa during the classical period.
After losing three presidential bids, this Chilean socialist finally won in 1970 — often called the first Marxist elected president in a liberal democracy in Latin America. Who was he?
Salvador Allende: President of Chile from 1970 to 1973.
Proclaimed in 1931 after King Alfonso XIII's ouster and toppled in 1939 by Franco's Nationalists, which democratic government ruled Spain through the Civil War era?
Second Spanish Republic: Government of Spain, 1931–1939. It was dissolved on 1 April 1939 after surrendering in the Spanish Civil War to the Nationalists rebels led by General Francisco Franco.
The longest-serving chief minister of Madhya Pradesh, this Indian politician later became national Minister of Agriculture and Farmers' Welfare in 2024 — who is he?
Holding the grim distinction of being the only British prime minister ever assassinated, this barrister was also the only attorney-general to reach the top job — who was he?
Spencer Perceval: Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1809 to 1812.

First emerging among Spanish and North American workers in the 1870s, this labor movement organizes workers by industry and uses strikes and direct action aiming to seize control of the means of production — what's it called?
A sickly, asthmatic child who built himself up through what he called 'the strenuous life,' he took office after McKinley's assassination as the youngest-ever president — who was he?
Theodore Roosevelt: President of the United States from 1901 to 1909.
Born a peasant, this man rose to become the most powerful figure in Japan and the first person ever to hold the rank of Kampaku without being born a noble — who was this second 'Great Unifier'?
Toyotomi Hideyoshi: Military ruler of Japan from 1585 to 1598.
Composed in an archaic Sanskrit dialect, this collection of four ancient hymn texts forms the oldest layer of Hindu scripture — what are they collectively called?
A former Fudan University law-school dean and professor of international politics, he became a leading Communist Party ideologist and now chairs the CPPCC — which Chinese politician?

Serving as both the last prime minister of Great Britain and the first of the United Kingdom, this statesman held office through the French Revolution and Napoleonic Wars, and was distinguished from his father, who shared his surname — who was he?
William Pitt the Younger: British statesman (1759–1806)
This Korean admiral won all of his roughly 23 naval battles against Japan, most famously defeating a fleet of over 130 ships with just 13 of his own — who is he?
Often called the 'Bismarck of Japan' for his realpolitik nation-building, this Satsuma-born statesman was one of three nobles who led the 1868 Meiji Restoration — who is he?
Which of these people was born first?
Ada Lovelace (born 1815) is the earliest of the four.
Who among these was born first?
Eratosthenes (born 276 BC) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four has been around longest?
COBOL (founded 1959) is the earliest of the four. COBOL (Common Business-Oriented Language;) is a compiled English-like computer programming language designed for business use.
Which of these was founded earliest?
C (programming language) (founded 1972) is the earliest of the four.
Pick the physicist from these four.
Joseph Henry is a physicist. Joseph Henry (December 17, 1797– May 13, 1878) was an American physicist and inventor who served as the first secretary of the Smithsonian Institution.
Which one below is best known as a mathematician?
What is the atomic number of Roentgenium?
Roentgenium (German: [ʁœntˈɡeːni̯ʊm]) is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Rg and atomic number 111.
What is the atomic number of Mercury?
Mercury is a chemical element; it has symbol Hg and atomic number 80.
In what year was Claudine Gay born?
Claudine Gay (born August 4, 1970) is an American political scientist who is the Wilbur A.
In what year was Louis Pasteur born?
Louis Pasteur: Pasteur's works are credited with saving millions of lives through the developments of vaccines for rabies and anthrax.
In what year was Isaac Newton born?
Isaac Newton: Newton contributed to and refined the scientific method, and his work is considered the most influential in bringing forth modern science.
In what year did Alexander Fleming die?
Alexander Fleming: Sir Alexander Fleming (6 August 1881 – 11 March 1955) was a Scottish physician and microbiologist.
In what year did John Maynard Keynes die?
John Maynard Keynes: Keynes was educated at King's College at the University of Cambridge, where he graduated in 1904 with a B.A. in mathematics.
In what year was Iron discovered?
Iron is a chemical element; it has symbol Fe (from Latin ferrum 'iron') and atomic number 26.
Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-25: Russian Aircraft Corporation MiG. Designed by the Soviet Union's Mikoyan-Gurevich bureau, it is an aircraft built primarily using stainless steel.
Which country is Aero L-39 Albatros from?
Aero L-39 Albatros: Czechoslovakia. The Aero L-39 Albatros is a high-performance jet trainer designed and produced by Aero Vodochody in the Czech Republic.
Who is credited with discovering Caelum?
Caelum: Nicolas Louis de Lacaille. Caelum SEE-ləm is a faint constellation in the southern sky, introduced in the 1750s by Nicolas Louis de Lacaille and counted among the 88 modern constellations.
Who is credited with discovering 243 Ida?
243 Ida: Johann Palisa. 243 Ida is an asteroid in the Koronis family of the asteroid belt.
Who is credited with discovering Gliese 581d?
Gliese 581d: Stéphane Udry. It was the third planet claimed in the system and the fourth (in a 4-planet model) or fifth (in a disproven 5- or 6-planet model) in order from the star.
Who is credited with discovering Chlorofluorocarbon?
Chlorofluorocarbon: Frédéric Swarts. The most common example of a CFC is dichlorodifluoromethane (R-12).

This Scottish physician's 1928 discovery of a mould-derived substance later named benzylpenicillin has been called the single greatest victory ever achieved over disease, and earned him a shared Nobel Prize in 1945 — who is he?
Alexander Fleming (6 August 1881 - 11 March 1955) was a Scottish physician and microbiologist.
This unit of length equals one ten-billionth of a meter, or 100 picometres, and is named after a 19th-century Swedish physicist — what is it?
Angstrom (ONG-) is a unit of length equal to 1010 m; that is, one ten-billionth of a metre, a hundred-millionth of a centimetre, 0.1 nanometre, or 100 picometres.

This type of blood vessel typically carries oxygen-rich blood away from the heart, though the vessels serving the lungs and an unborn baby's placenta carry deoxygenated blood instead — what's it called?
Artery (from Greek (artr)) is a blood vessel in humans and most other animals that takes oxygenated blood away from the heart in the systemic circulation to one or more parts of the body.

This genus of deciduous trees includes 14 species across two subgenera, one found only in East Asia with low, multi-trunked growth, the other spanning Europe, Asia, and eastern North America. What tree genus is this?

Beech (genus Fagus) is a genus of deciduous trees in the family Fagaceae, native to subtropical (accessory forest element) and temperate (as dominant element of mesophytic forests) Eurasia and North America.

Believed to descend from hounds kept at a Belgian abbey and used by police worldwide to track escaped prisoners, this scent hound can discern a person's trail days after they've passed — name this dog breed?
Bloodhound is a large scent hound, originally bred for hunting deer, wild boar, rabbits, and since the Middle Ages, for tracking people.

This opioid medication used to treat addiction and pain can be delivered under the tongue, through the cheek, by injection, patch, or implant — and is often combined with naloxone to deter misuse — what drug is it?
Buprenorphine is an opioid used to treat opioid use disorder, acute pain, and chronic pain.
Which Mediterranean evergreen tree, grown mainly in Spain, produces edible seed pods often ground into a chocolate substitute, with seeds that yield a gum used as a food thickener?
Carob (Ceratonia siliqua) is a flowering evergreen tree or shrub in the Caesalpinioideae subfamily of the legume family, Fabaceae.
The principal sterol of all animals, it concentrates in the brain and spinal cord and is essential to every cell membrane — yet too much in the blood spells trouble. What is it?
Cholesterol is the principal sterol of all animals, distributed in body tissues, especially the brain and spinal cord, and in animal fats and oils.

The most widely distributed corvid, this large all-black bird is found across the Northern Hemisphere and is the heaviest passerine bird, with 11 accepted subspecies showing little variation in appearance. What bird is this?
Common raven (Corvus corax) is a large all-black passerine bird.
The third most-produced American fighter of the Second World War, trailing only the Mustang and the Thunderbolt, this plane first took flight in 1938 — which aircraft?
Curtiss P-40 Warhawk is an American single-engined, single-seat, all-metal fighter-bomber that first flew in 1938.
First discovered in 1877 and named the following year for its unique double-beamed tail bones, this genus of long-necked sauropod dinosaur roamed Late Jurassic North America — what is it?
Diplodocus (or) is an extinct genus of diplodocid sauropod dinosaurs known from the Late Jurassic of North America.
A onetime clerk for Justice Thurgood Marshall, this Harvard Law School dean was tapped for the Supreme Court by President Obama in 2010 — who is she?
Elena Kagan (born April 28, 1960) is an American lawyer who serves as an associate justice of the Supreme Court of the United States.
This U.S. Marine turned professor wrote a 1981 memoir of his WWII combat, later adapted into a Ken Burns documentary and an HBO miniseries where he was played by Joseph Mazzello — who was he?
Eugene Sledge (November 4, 1923 - March 3, 2001) was a United States Marine, university professor, and author.
This infection and inflammation of hair follicles produces white-tipped pimples anywhere on hair-covered skin, and is considered a distinct condition from acne. Name it?
Folliculitis is the infection and inflammation of one or more hair follicles.
This branch of medicine has no set starting age, instead guided by a patient's needs and available caregiving, and helps those managing multiple chronic conditions — what is it?
Geriatrics is a medical specialty focused on addressing the unique health needs of older adults.

This German physicist turned his eye on the mind itself, founding psychophysics and giving his name to a law showing that sensation rises with the logarithm — not the raw intensity — of a stimulus. Whose pioneering work was it?
Gustav Fechner (19 April 1801 - 18 November 1887) was a German physicist, philosopher, and experimental psychologist.
Sometimes called urticaria, this itchy rash of raised welts can flare for minutes or days, may follow an allergy or infection, and in half of all cases has no identifiable cause — what is it?
Hives is a kind of skin rash with red or flesh-colored, raised, itchy bumps.

For decades this University of Virginia psychiatrist ran a Division of Perceptual Studies and gathered evidence that memories — and even bodily features — might carry across lives. Which researcher into reincarnation was he?

Ian Stevenson (October 31, 1918 - February 8, 2007) was a Canadian-born American psychiatrist, the founder and director of the Division of Perceptual Studies at the University of Virginia School of Medicine.
This Canadian-American physical educator invented an entire sport, wrote its original rule book after moving to the United States, and founded the University of Kansas's program in 1898 — who is he?
James Naismith (November 6, 1861 - November 28, 1939) was a Canadian-American physical educator, physician, Christian chaplain, and sports coach, best known as the inventor of the game of basketball.
Endemic to New Caledonia's mountain forests, this bluish-grey, nearly flightless bird sports bright red legs and unique nasal corns shared by no other bird — what is it?
Kagu (Rhynochetos jubatus) is a crested, long-legged, and bluish-grey bird endemic to the dense mountain forests of New Caledonia.
The last member of the actinide series, this synthetic element is named for the inventor of the cyclotron — which element holds atomic number 103?
Lawrencium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Lr (formerly Lw) and atomic number 103.

Built by an American defense contractor with partners including Northrop Grumman and BAE Systems, this single-engine, single-seat stealth fighter comes in conventional, short-takeoff, and carrier-launched variants — name the aircraft?
Lockheed Martin F-35 Lightning II is an American family of single-seat, single-engine, supersonic stealth strike fighters.
An economist by training, he became the only Sikh to lead India and the first prime minister since Nehru to be re-appointed after a full five-year term — who is he?
Manmohan Singh (26 September 1932 - 26 December 2024) was an Indian economist, bureaucrat, academician and statesman who served as the prime minister of India from 2004 to 2014.

Sold in Europe as part of a blended sedative called Mandrax alongside an antihistamine, this sedative-hypnotic drug of the quinazolinone class was pulled from many markets in the 1980s due to widespread misuse — name this compound?
Methaqualone is a sedative-hypnotic medication that was widely prescribed during the mid-20th century.
Their name means "little fly" in Spanish, and biologists class them as micropredators — all sip flower nectar, but the females of many species also drink blood. What are they?
Mosquito are a family of small flies consisting of 3,600 species.
Named for a pioneering physicist's work on classical mechanics, this SI unit of force equals the push needed to accelerate one kilogram at one metre per second squared — name the unit?
Newton (unit) (symbol: N) is the unit of force in the International System of Units (SI).
Its name means 'serpent-bearer' in Ancient Greek — this large constellation straddling the celestial equator is depicted as a man grasping a snake — name it?
Ophiuchus (o-fee-) is a large constellation straddling the celestial equator.
A physician in this medical field — devoted to the study of disease and diagnosing it largely by analyzing tissue and cell samples — is called a pathologist. What is the field?
Pathology is the study of disease. The word pathology also refers to the study of disease in general, incorporating a wide range of biology research fields and medical practices.
Ranging in color from clear to yellow, green, or even grey, this respiratory mucus is expelled through coughing and also goes by the name sputum — what is it?
Phlegm (Ancient) is mucus produced by the respiratory system, excluding that produced by the throat and nose passages.
Abundant throughout the plant kingdom, this broad class of naturally occurring phenolic compounds includes flavonoids and ellagitannin — what is the family called?
Polyphenol are a large family of naturally occurring phenols.

This psychiatric state describes an inability to distinguish reality from delusion, marked by symptoms like hallucinations and disorganized thinking, and can stem from conditions like schizophrenia or bipolar disorder — name the state?
Psychosis is the inability to distinguish what is or is not real.
One of the three ancient arts of discourse alongside grammar and logic, this discipline studies the techniques speakers and writers use to inform, persuade, and motivate an audience — what is it?
Rhetoric is the art of persuasion.
Contracted from contaminated food, this bacterial illness typically causes diarrhea, fever, and cramps within a day or two of exposure — what is it called?
Salmonellosis is a symptomatic infection caused by bacteria of the genus Salmonella.
This Pakistani-American businessman owns both an NFL franchise, the Jacksonville Jaguars, and an English Premier League club, Fulham — who is he?
Shahid Khan (born July 18, 1950) is a Pakistani and American businessman.
The largest of the toothed whales and the largest toothed predator alive, this pelagic giant has females who give birth only every four to twenty years — what is it?
Sperm whale (Physeter macrocephalus) is the largest of the toothed whales and the largest toothed predator.
Educated in Rotterdam through World War II, this Indonesian economist later served as minister of finance, trade, and research under two different presidents — who was he?
Sumitro Djojohadikusumo (27 May 1917 - 9 March 2001) was an Indonesian statesman and one of the country's most influential economists.
Enhanced by painted scenery and stagecraft like lighting, this live performing art shares its name with the very buildings where its shows are staged — what is it?

Theatre is a collaborative form of performing art that uses live performers, usually actors, to present experiences of a real or imagined event before a live audience in a specific place, often a stage.

This invasive annual plant, native to warm regions of Eurasia and Africa but now found in North America and Australia, produces small woody burrs with sharp spines capable of piercing bare feet. What plant is this?
Tribulus terrestris is an annual plant in the caltrop family (Zygophyllaceae) widely distributed around the world.
Its Latin name means 'maiden,' and it's the largest zodiac grouping in the sky, home to the bright star Spica between Leo and Libra — which one?
Virgo (constellation) is one of the constellations of the zodiac. The ecliptic intersects the celestial equator within this constellation and Pisces.

This Greek economist served as Finance Minister under PM Alexis Tsipras during the 2015 debt crisis, becoming internationally known for opposing EU-imposed austerity, before co-founding the left-wing party DiEM25 — who is he?
Yanis Varoufakis (born 24 March 1961) is a Greek economist, academic, author, and politician.

Nicknamed wolfsbane, monkshood, and devil's helmet, this highly toxic genus of over 250 mountain-dwelling flowering plants thrives in moist, well-draining soils across the Northern Hemisphere — what is it?
Aconitum: Genus of flowering plants in the buttercup family Ranunculaceae.
Which Swiss chemist was the first person to synthesize and personally experience the effects of LSD, later isolating the active compounds in magic mushrooms?
Named for its males' mating call, which sounds like a farm animal bellowing, this large amphibian native to eastern North America has been introduced worldwide as a food source — which species?
American bullfrog: Species of amphibian. It typically inhabits large permanent water bodies such as swamps, ponds, and lakes.

Characterized by extreme food restriction and a fear of gaining weight despite being underweight, this eating disorder is described in the DSM-5 as involving a disturbance in how one perceives their own body shape — what's the condition called?
Anorexia nervosa: Eating disorder. Individuals with anorexia nervosa have a fear of gaining weight, despite the fact that they are typically underweight.
The third most abundant gas in Earth's atmosphere at nearly 1%, this noble gas takes its name from an Ancient Greek word meaning 'lazy' or 'inactive' — what element is it?
Argon: Chemical element with atomic number 18 (Ar)
From the Greek for "self-devouring," this lysosome-driven process lets a cell tidily break down and recycle its own worn-out parts — what is it?
Autophagy: Process of cells digesting parts of themselves.
Spurred by the 1980 failure of Operation Eagle Claw, this American tiltrotor blends a helicopter's vertical takeoff with a turboprop's long-range cruise — what aircraft is it?
Bell Boeing V-22 Osprey: Military transport tiltrotor.
Rich in vitamin C and polyphenols, this deciduous shrub's glossy dark berries are cooked into jams and syrups or fermented into cassis — what is it?
Blackcurrant: Species of flowering plant in the gooseberry family Grossulariaceae.

This infraorder of decapod crustaceans tucks a stubby tail-like abdomen under a hard shell and ends its front pair of legs in pincers — over 1.5 million tonnes of them are eaten by humans yearly. What group is it?
Brachyura: Crustacean. The true crabs are the largest of the crab decapod groups with carcinised body forms.
A cole crop related to broccoli, cauliflower and Brussels sprouts, the heaviest recorded head of this leafy vegetable weighed nearly 138 pounds — what is it?
Cabbage: Leafy vegetable in the flowering plant family Brassicaceae.
This infraorder of decapod crustaceans is the true taxonomic home of what everyone actually calls a shrimp, found in fresh and salt water worldwide — what is it?
The largest part of the brain, this structure houses the cerebral cortex plus the hippocampus and basal ganglia, and works with the cerebellum to control every voluntary action. What is it?
Cerebrum: Large part of the brain containing the cerebral cortex.
This Dutch scientist discovered Saturn's largest moon and invented the pendulum clock, the most accurate timekeeper for nearly three centuries — who is he?
Christiaan Huygens: Dutch mathematician and physicist (1629–1695)
Nicknamed the 'palm thief,' this giant terrestrial arthropod can weigh over 9 pounds, making it the largest land-dwelling arthropod alive today — what is it?
Thanks to a variation in the gene OR6A2, some people taste this herb — called cilantro in the US — as fresh and citrusy while others swear it tastes like soap. What is it?
Coriander: Annual herb. Coriander, or Coriandrum sativum, is an annual herb in the family Apiaceae.
Once sold under the brand name Flexeril and chemically similar to tricyclic antidepressants, this oral medication treats sudden muscle spasms — what's the drug?
Cyclobenzaprine: Muscle relaxant medication. It should not be used together with MAOIs.
Caused by about 40 types of fungus and often picked up in public showers or contact sports like wrestling, this infection produces a red, itchy, scaly circular rash — what is it?
Dermatophytosis: Fungus infection of the skin. Dermatophytosis, also known as tinea and ringworm, is a fungal infection of the skin (a dermatomycosis), that may affect skin, hair, and nails.

Originally developed to compete for a USAF aerial-tanker contract it lost to Boeing's Stratotanker, this four-engined jetliner instead entered airline service with Delta in 1959 — what aircraft was it?
Douglas DC-8: American four-engined jet airliner family.
Capable of delivering shocks up to 860 volts, this South American knifefish helped inspire the invention of the battery in 1800 — what is it?
Electric eel: Genus of fishes in South America.
Also called rocket or arugula, this sharp-flavored leaf vegetable native to the Mediterranean and Asia is a popular salad green in the cabbage family — which plant?
This burrowing mammal builds ever-expanding tunnel systems, and its saliva contains toxins that paralyze its favorite prey, earthworms — what animal is it?
European mole: Species of mammal. The European mole (Talpa europaea) is a mammal of the order Eulipotyphla.
Historically used in the 18th century to track down escaped slaves, this large Brazilian dog breed of mastiff type now also serves as a guard dog and companion — which breed?
Fila Brasileiro: Brazilian breed of dog. The Fila Brasileiro (Portuguese pronunciation: [ˈfilɐ bɾaziˈlejɾu]) is a Brazilian breed of large working dog of mastiff type.
Also called the Baader-Meinhof phenomenon or Red Car Theory, this cognitive bias makes you notice something everywhere right after you first learn about it — what is it?
Frequency illusion: Kind of cognitive bias. The name "Baader–Meinhof phenomenon" was coined in 1994 by Terry Mullen in a letter to the St.

Germany's first professor of experimental physics is remembered both for the tree-like electrical discharge patterns named after him and for the witty posthumous notebooks he called "waste books" — who was he?
Georg Christoph Lichtenberg: German scientist and satirist (1742–1799)
Known online by the alias 'anakata,' this Swedish computer specialist co-founded a notorious BitTorrent site and later helped WikiLeaks with its 2010 release of a leaked military video — who is he?
Gottfrid Svartholm: Swedish computer specialist. Parts of an interview with Svartholm commenting on the May 2006 police raid of The Pirate Bay are featured in Good Copy Bad Copy and Steal This Film.
Nicknamed the slime eel, this jawless marine scavenger is the only living animal with a skull but no proper backbone — what is it?
Hagfish: Class of eel-shaped, slime-producing animal.

Famous for the ideas of "bounded rationality" and "satisficing," this remarkable scholar won both a Turing Award and a Nobel in Economics — bridging computer science, economics, and psychology. Who was he?
Herbert A. Simon: American academic and Nobel Laureate (1916–2001)

Found only in the Americas from Alaska to Tierra del Fuego, these roughly 375 species pull off rapid, maneuverable flight thanks to an exceptional metabolism — and their males flaunt the widest plumage diversity of any bird — what are they?
This Russian-American engineer built the first successful four-engine aircraft in 1913 and went on to pioneer the modern helicopter — who was he?
Nicknamed 'Dr. Death,' this pathologist assisted at least 130 patients in dying and was convicted of murder after broadcasting one such case on television — who is he?
Jack Kevorkian: American pathologist and euthanasia activist (1928–2011)
The youngest division chief in GM history shepherded the Pontiac GTO before founding the motor company behind a stainless-steel sports car immortalized in Back to the Future — who was he?
John DeLorean: American automobile engineer and executive (1925–2005)
Sold under names like Toradol and Acular, this NSAID's use is capped at five days due to serious side-effect risk, with relief starting within an hour — what drug is it?
Known by common names like true lavender and English lavender despite not being native to England, this Mediterranean-basin plant belongs to the mint family — which species?
Lavandula angustifolia: Species of plant. Lavandula angustifolia, formerly L. officinalis, is a flowering plant in the family Lamiaceae, native to the Mediterranean basin.
Also known as the deer ked, this blood-sucking fly sheds its own wings once it lands on a host and burrows through the fur to feed — what species is it?
Lipoptena cervi: Species of fly. Lipoptena cervi, the deer ked or deer fly, is a species of biting fly in the family of louse flies, Hippoboscidae.
This common, nonspecific medical sign involves lymph nodes becoming abnormally swollen or enlarged, with causes ranging from the common cold to cancer. What's the condition called?
Lymphadenopathy: Abnormal change in size of the lymph nodes.
A student of Marie Curie, this French physicist discovered the element francium in 1939 and later became the first woman elected to the French Académie des Sciences — who was she?
Typically occurring between ages 45 and 55, this natural decline in estrogen and progesterone permanently ends a woman's menstrual periods?
Menopause: Time when menstrual periods stop permanently.

NATO called it 'Farmer,' and this Soviet twin-engine fighter was the first Soviet production aircraft capable of supersonic speed in level flight, later battling American jets over North Vietnam — which aircraft?
Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-19: Air superiority fighter aircraft family.
Nicknamed noni, this pungent-smelling fruit tree in the coffee family was spread across the Pacific by Polynesian sailors and is now used mainly in traditional medicine and juices — which plant?
Morinda citrifolia: Species of plant. It is commonly known as noni or Indian mulberry, among many other names.
Made of two fused benzene rings, this pungent white crystalline compound is the main ingredient in traditional mothballs — what is it?
Naphthalene: Chemical compound. It is a white crystalline solid with a characteristic odor that is detectable at concentrations as low as 0.08 ppm.
Element 102 honors the inventor of dynamite, who endowed a famous set of prizes — fitting, since this synthetic metal can only be forged in particle accelerators. What is it?
Nobelium: Chemical element with atomic number 102 (No)
Causing white or yellow discoloration, thickening, and lifting of the nail — and far more often striking toenails than fingernails — what is this fungal infection also called tinea unguium?
Named by Reginald Innes Pocock in 1917 to cover big cats of genus Panthera, this cat subfamily later grew to include the clouded leopards too — which subfamily?
Pantherinae: Subfamily of felids. The Pantherinae genetically diverged from a common ancestor between 9.32 to 4.47 million years ago and 10.67 to 3.76 million years ago.
Harvested from Penicillium moulds and brewed in deep tanks, this β-lactam was among the first medicines to knock out staph and strep infections. What is it?
Penicillin: Group of antibiotics derived from fungi.

So reactive that it never appears uncombined in nature, this element was famously isolated in 1669 by Hennig Brand — the scientific community's first documented discovery of an element — and comes in white and red forms. Which one is it?
Phosphorus: Chemical element with atomic number 15 (P)
This plant process moves pollen from an anther to a stigma, eventually letting a tube grow down the style to reach the ovary and enable fertilization. What is it?
Pollination: Biological process occurring in plants.
Discovered in 1915, this red dwarf is the closest star to Earth besides the Sun, orbiting its two larger neighbors once every 550,000 years — which star?
Proxima Centauri: Nearest star to the Solar System.
Used to treat malaria resistant to chloroquine, this bitter compound also flavors tonic water and can cause ringing in the ears at high doses — what is it?
Quinine: Medication used to treat malaria and babesiosis.
With the widest geographic range of any non-human primate, this brown-to-grey Old World monkey lives in matrilineal troops of up to 200 individuals — which species?
Rhesus macaque: Species of Old World monkey. The rhesus macaque (Macaca mulatta), colloquially rhesus monkey, is a species of Old World monkey in the Macaca genus.
What term describes herbivorous mammals like cattle and giraffes that digest plant matter by regurgitating and re-chewing it as cud?
Ruminant: Hoofed herbivorous grazing or browsing mammals.
About 90% of cases trace to a herniated spinal disc pressing on a nerve root, producing a shooting pain that runs from the lower back down one leg — what's the condition?
Sciatica: Lower-back pain that can extend down the leg.
Nicknamed the 'brushwood dog' for its game-flushing hunting style, this is the smallest of Japan's six native dog breeds — which breed?
Shiba Inu: Japanese dog breed. The Shiba Inu (Japanese: 柴犬; Japanese pronunciation: [ɕi.ba.i.nɯ]) is a breed of hunting dog from Japan.

Originating in South America and rapidly diversifying after the extinction of the dinosaurs, this plant family — commonly known as the nightshades — includes toxic alkaloid-rich species alongside tomatoes, potatoes, and peppers. What family is it?
Built from four fused carbon rings, this class of organic compounds includes cholesterol, testosterone, and anabolic performance-enhancers — what is it called?
Steroid: Polycyclic organic compound having sterane as a core structure.

Caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum, this infection famously hides: a painless ulcer first, then a rash that loves the palms and soles, then years of silent latency before tertiary damage. What is it?

This congenital heart defect combines four distinct abnormalities — including a hole between the ventricles and a narrowed pulmonary exit — and can trigger cyanotic 'spells' in infants — what is this condition?
Tetralogy of Fallot: Type of congenital heart defect. Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF), formerly known as Steno-Fallot tetralogy, is a congenital heart defect characterized by four specific cardiac defects.
This white compound found in sunscreen, paint, and food coloring under the number E171 makes up two-thirds of all pigments used worldwide and is valued at over $13 billion — what is it?
Titanium dioxide: Chemical compound. Titanium dioxide, also known as titanium(IV) oxide or titania, is the inorganic compound derived from titanium with the chemical formula TiO2.

These simple-looking marine invertebrates surprise biologists: their tadpole-like larvae sport a notochord and dorsal nerve cord, making them startlingly close kin to vertebrates. What are these chordates?
Tunicate: Marine animals, subphylum of chordates.
